Promotes public accountability and good governance in Tanzania through policy advocacy, research, capacity building, and citizen engagement. The mission is also to apply Public Social Accountability Monitoring (PSAM) analytical tool to ensure that there is proper public resources management and good governance in the country.

Promotes public accountability and good governance in Tanzania through policy advocacy, research, capacity building, and citizen engagement. The mission is also to apply Public Social Accountability Monitoring (PSAM) analytical tool to ensure that there is proper public resources management and good governance in the country.
Expected outcomes of the program are: i)To strengthen citizen engagement in demanding Public Finance Accountability (PFA) ii)To enhance capacity of media, youth, CSOs, duty bearers and elected representatives in the practice of PFA iii)To influence policy change in improving the environment of PFA iii)To strengthen Wajibus technical and financial capacity towards making it as an effective public finance accountability think tank institution.
To achieve these outcomes mentioned above, the program will support the capacity development of civil society (users committees, local NGOs, youth, media, duty bearers and elected representatives) to implement and promote the principles of public finance accountability. Beyond, it will help establish effective collaborative links between civil society, local elected officials and technical services to ensure their participation in decision-making. As it will be better informed, civil society and the citizens will be well prepared to negotiate the inclusion during budgeting and spending of public finances.

title.narrative: Amendment number 2 to the grant agreement between Sida and Wajibu.
Wajibu Institute of Public Accountability Strategic Plan 2021-2025

description.narrative:
.Wajibu Institute of Accountability has submitted its annual narrative report which they call it 'Performance program report'. It is the final report expected from them as there is no any fund left in their bank account from Sweden.
One specific element I will include in this report this time is the inclusion of page numbers for the results that I have picked for assessment in this particular section. The reason for that is to provide room for whoever wanting to make reference, or wanting to read the original report.
The results are many and all of them are excellent to report on but I have chosen a few for now across their 4 objectives from strategic plan.
Objective 1: To strengthen citizens understanding of accountability issues through CSOs engagement resulting in demanding for more transparency and accountability in the country 2025
According to WAJIBU, it is reported that citizens have shifted from passive listeners to active participants and that was enabled through interactive radio programs featuring live debates, SMS engagement, and community discussions questioning leaders in demand of transparency and accountability in the collection and use of public resources. According to the 2025 report, during the monitoring period, journalists and community members collectively tracked 35 public projects valued at approximately TZS 6.97 billion, identifying service delivery gaps and preventing further waste of public funds. According to Wajibu, he initiative generated tangible improvements in health service delivery, particularly by addressing facilities that had been completed but remained non-operational: For example, Simbo Health Centre in Kigoma (valued at TZS 500 million) began providing services within a month after being highlighted in a live radio debate. Page 10, Annual performance Report 2025.
Objective 2: To enhance capacity of Strategic stakeholders in the practice of Public Financial Accountability by 2025.
Wajibu Institute of Accountability chose strategic partners to engage with during implementation of their new strategic plan. The choices included specific district councils and committes of community members who would continuously engage for the purposes of improving service delivery. For example, Wajibu is reporting that, in the Uvinza District Councils at the Ruchugi Village, the village PETS committee observed oversight and transparency challenges in two primary schools of Kazaroho and Muungano. At Kazaroho Primary School, the head teacher misused public funds meant for the construction of new toilet facilities. Due to poor involvement of the school management committee and lack of transparency, the toilets were substandard and showed structural cracks even before their completion. The schools PETS committee took action by tracking the project, reporting on the issues to the district education department. The head teacher who misused the funds was suspended and demoted, and it was ordered to reconstruct the toilets at his own expense and in accordance with the government standards under strict supervision.
Another example is reported from Muungano Primary School, the schools PETS tool uncovered the unauthorized construction of five business kiosks which began in 2022 within the school compound which had been done unprocedural and did not involve the community. These five business kiosks were corruptly and illegally constructed with permanent fixtures on the schools playground field by a few shrewd and corrupt business people. Again, the schools PETS committee, in collaboration with TAWEA (WAjibu's partner at the village) and WAJIBU, conducted community meeting dialogues that uncovered severe mis-management and poor oversight of the schools funds. This resulted in the dismantling of the illegally constructed kiosks to restore the playground field to the pupils and thereby reinforced the need for proper oversight at the school. This also triggered significant community and administrative actions, leading to improved governance and accountability in public education projects across the district. page 17 and 16
Another notable example of impact emerged in Mpimbwe District, where a journalist investigated the long-delayed completion of Luchima Dispensary, an issue previously highlighted in the 2023/24 CAG reports. Following media exposure in June and July 2025, authorities responded by renovating the facility, painting, tiling, and installing windows and doors and deploying nurses, medicines, and medical equipment. By November 2025, journalists and CACs from Luchima village confirmed that construction of the dispensarys toilets was nearing completion, enabling the community to begin accessing essential health services from the facility. Again, impreesions by Swedish Embassy is that, community actions will continue and thus giving accountability legitimacy.
Objective 3: To advocate for and proactively influence public financial accountability policies for implementation and/or change in 2025.
It is reported that Wajibu's engagement with PPRA, CAG, PCCB, IAG, and OCAGZ, proposed policy reforms to strengthen the Public Financial Management (PFM) framework and practices which were reviewed and endorsed. Below is an evidence of a section of the law that got changed due to Wajibu's engagement. The engagement contributed to selected PFM policy reforms such as the amendment of section 31(2) of the Public Finance Act 2001 which shortened the timeframe for Accounting Officers to prepare and submit the financial statements to the CAG by 31st August instead of 30th September each year. According to Wajibu, the shortening of the timeframe enables the Controller and Auditor General (CAG) to present the Annual Audit Reports to the President by 31st December, thereby enhancing the timeliness and relevance of audit findings for public scrutiny and policy action.
Objective 4: Strengthening WAJIBUs Technical and Financial Capacity as an Effective Public Finance Accountability (PFA) Think-Tank
WAJIBUs managed to strengthen its operational and human resource capacity to effectively deliver on its mandate. The organization invested over TZS 360 million in essential working tools, including ICT equipment, office furniture, and a new motor vehicle, significantly improving staff productivity, mobility, and working conditions across Mainland and Zanzibar offices. Complementing these investments, it is reported that, WAJIBU enhanced staff competencies through structured capacity-building initiatives. All staff participated in targeted training in areas such as digital and strategic communication, monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL), and institutional policy compliance. The combination of improved infrastructure and skilled personnel has strengthened WAJIBUs technical capacity to deliver high-quality research, analysis, and advisory services in PFA.page 23
Few challenges are highlighted by Wajibu's report, challenges - In some communities, youths were reported to be very skeptical whether raising concerns would lead into any action or arrest. Further Wajibu's report says that youths in the accountability clubs were facing fear of airing their views and voices regarding the misuse of public resources. Funding challenges are also mentioned by Wajibu as donors sweden in this case being the largest closed its support with short notice as thus pausing huge challenges beyond 2025. page24
Some good hopes are also reported for the future, - The existence of a good working relationship between WAJIBU, government institutions and the media has enabled WAJIBU to implement its advocacy agenda in shaping the PFM trajectory in the country. WAJIBU thnks that will leverage on the good reputation with the government and development partners toreengage for anti corruption and accountability work in Tanzania.
This being the final year, Embassy of Sweden assesses that lots of good achievements have been recorded by working with WAJIBU. More could be accomplished but directives from Sweden changed the length of partnership with WAJIBU. AS PO I feel proud to have worked with WAJIBU, the only CSO in Tanzania working to improve public finance management practices in Tanzania. Swedish contribution will be remembered in communities, schools and systems where changes were realized.
